reason: A five-word run opening the verse, and it is a false friend of an unusually exact kind. “all this was done” occurs in exactly three KJV verses — Matthew 1:22, 21:4 and 26:56 — and in all three it is the front half of a fulfilment formula: 'that it might be fulfilled which was spoken of the Lord by the prophet', 'that the scriptures of the prophets might be fulfilled'. The clause exists in the KJV only to attach an event to a prophecy. 3 Nephi 7:5 uses the identical words to attach the event to a cause of the opposite kind: 'Now all this was done, and there was no wars as yet among them; and all this iniquity had come upon the people, because they did yield themselves unto the power of satan.' Matthew's formula explains a happening by God's word; the Book of Mormon's explains it by Satan's power. Nothing else of Matthew 1 is present, and the Book of Mormon has its own fulfilment formula ('that the word might be fulfilled') which it does not use here.

The strongest string match in the first half of the chapter after the dog and the sow, and it inverts. “entered into a covenant” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, 2 Chronicles 15:12 and Ezekiel 16:8, and the Chronicles verse continues with the infinitive of purpose the Book of Mormon also has — 'entered into a covenant to seek the LORD God of their fathers'. But 3 Nephi 7:11's covenanters have 'entered into a covenant to destroy the government', and they are the object of the sentence's hatred, not its subject: the tribes are 'united in the hatred of those who had entered into a covenant'. Asa's covenant is a national oath to seek God, sworn publicly and enforced on pain of death; this is the secret combination's oath to destroy a government, and 7:6 has already named it 'the secret combination'. The catalogue does have a link to Asa's covenant assembly, and it is a good one — Alma 46:35, where the whole structure of 2 Chronicles 15:8-15 is rebuilt including the death penalty for refusing the oath. A reader who arrives at 3 Nephi 7:11 by way of that row should be told that the phrase here is the same and the covenant is its opposite.

sharedText: (a kingdom in the north obtained by flattery)
reason: Typology pulls hard here and the wording will not bear it — the Exodus 2:2 'goodly' entry in 1 Nephi is the model for this kind of refusal. Daniel 11:21 is the King James Bible's one portrait of a man who is not entitled to a kingdom and gets one anyway: 'in his estate shall stand up a vile person, to whom they shall not give the honour of the kingdom: but he shall come in peaceably, and obtain the kingdom by flatteries.' 3 Nephi 7:9-12 crowns a man the tribes have not chosen, over a band rather than a nation, who takes flight 'into the northernmost part of the land, and there build up unto themselves a kingdom' — Daniel 11's king of the north, established by flattery. The verbal case collapses on inspection. “flatteries” occurs in exactly three KJV verses, all of them in Daniel 11 (21, 32, 34), and the Book of Mormon does not use the word: “flattered” occurs in exactly zero KJV verses, and the Book of Mormon's clause is 'he flattered them that there would be many dissenters', which is flattery used to recruit, not to corrupt. No other word of Daniel 11:21 is present. Recorded so that a reader who sees the type is told the catalogue saw it and declined it.

sharedText: in the thirty and first year
reason: A six-word run and the highest n-gram score in the second half of the chapter, and it is arithmetic. “thirty and first year” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Kings 16:23, for the simple reason that the KJV dates by regnal year constantly and had occasion to write this particular numeral once. 1 Kings 16:23 is the accession of Omri; 3 Nephi 7:14 is a year in the Nephite reckoning from the sign of Christ's birth, and the same book dates its chapters this way throughout (7:1, 7:13, 7:21, 7:23, 7:26 and onward). The candidate ranks again at 7:21 and is covered here rather than listed twice. This entry follows the standing treatment of regnal dating filed at Helaman 1:1.

A five-word run scoring 2.00, and the coincidence is grammatical rather than lexical: the Book of Mormon's clause is 'they were established according to the minds of them which was their chiefs and their leaders', where 'the minds of' means the opinions of the tribal leaders and 'them which' is the ordinary 1830 relative that 1920 changed to 'those who'. 2 Corinthians 4:4 is about minds blinded by the god of this world. The Pauline verse is nevertheless in this chapter, two verses later and in its proper sense: see the link at 7:16, where 'the blindness of their minds' fuses 2 Corinthians 4:4's blinded minds with Ephesians 4:18's blindness of heart. The run here is a decoy that happens to point at the right epistle for the wrong reason.

“written in this book” occurs in exactly twelve KJV verses, of which 2 Kings 23:3 is one and five are Deuteronomic curse formulae; in all of the Old Testament instances the book in question is the book of the law and the point is that its contents bind. 3 Nephi 7:17's point is the reverse — what is not in the book. The negative form settles it: “not written in this book” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 20:30, and that is where the link is written.

The chapter's most tempting silent parallel. 3 Nephi 7:19 says that Nephi, in the name of Jesus, 'even his brother did he raise from the dead, after he had been stoned and suffered death by the people' — and the King James Bible has exactly one narrative of a named man raised from the dead whom the text repeatedly identifies as somebody's brother, John 11, where Lazarus is 'the brother' of Mary and Martha at 11:2, 11:19, 11:21, 11:23 and 11:32. The verbal contact is nil. “raise from the dead” occurs in exactly zero KJV verses; John 11:44 reads 'And he that was dead came forth, bound hand and foot with graveclothes'; the Book of Mormon supplies a stoning that John has no counterpart for, and its raised man is the raiser's own brother rather than a friend's. What is worth recording, and is recorded at 7:17 instead, is that the sentence sits inside a passage built on John's two colophons — so a reader who feels John's presence here is feeling something real and finding it in the wrong verse.

The same five-word window ranks at 7:21, 7:22 and 7:25 and is the commonest candidate in the chapter, which is exactly what a connective run does. Acts 14:18 is 'with these sayings scarce restrained they the people, that they had not done sacrifice unto them' — the crowd at Lystra being talked out of offering to Barnabas and Paul. The Book of Mormon's three occurrences are 'did truly signify unto the people that they had been visited', 'did truly manifest unto the people that they had been wrought upon', and 'unto the people, that they had repented'. In every case the words are the seam between a verb of declaring and its content clause, and the seam is the whole of the match. Covered here for all three verses under the standing exclusion for connective runs (CONVENTIONS §5).

Not a machine candidate but worth catching by eye, because the arithmetic is inviting: “evil spirits and infirmities” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 8:2, and that verse also has devils going out of a woman, so it holds in a single clause both halves of 3 Nephi 7:22's 'as many as had devils cast out from them, and were healed of their sicknesses and their infirmities'. The singleton is not reproduced. The Book of Mormon has 'sicknesses and their infirmities' where Luke has 'evil spirits and infirmities', and “their infirmities” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Luke 5:15 and 7:21, neither of them Luke 8:2 — so the phrase the Book of Mormon actually writes points at two other verses than the one the rare pairing suggested. The verse is adjudicated instead as part of the Mark 16:17-20 signs-list borrowing recorded at 7:19, where 7:22 is listed in recurrenceRefs; Luke 8:2 is carried there as a composite rather than made the source.

A five-word run whose next words diverge completely — 2 Chronicles 30:17 continues 'in the congregation that were not sanctified', 3 Nephi 7:26 'in the commencement of this year, that were baptized unto repentance'. The Chronicles verse is about Levites killing passover lambs for the ritually unclean at Hezekiah's passover; the Book of Mormon verse is a year-end tally of converts. The only tie is the existential 'there were many in the', which is bare English.

Filed as a figural link when this chapter was adjudicated, with an explicit withdrawal condition: 'Withdraw this row if the 3 Nephi 10:5 quotation of Matthew 23:37 turns out on adjudication to be independent of chapter 7.' It has. 3 Nephi 10:4-5 quotes Matthew 23:37 on its own verbal evidence — mediation-check.py decides Matthew over Luke 13:34 on two independent points (“gathereth” not “doth gather”, “chickens” not “brood”) — with no reference to this verse. The structural observation stands and is recorded at 3 Nephi 10:4's recurrenceRefs (which lists 3 Nephi 7:14 is not among them, correctly: 7:14 shares no wording with Matthew 23:37 at all, only the narrative fact of prophets stoned). Stoning prophets is a commonplace of the prophetic literature (2 Chronicles 24:21, Hebrews 11:37) and the Book of Mormon has its own idiom for it; there is nothing left to attach a link to once the structural argument is withdrawn.
